title: New Scientist Story Ideas — Bipolar — September 2026

studies.title: Genes for addiction — not for drinking or smoking as such — explain why bipolar disorder and substance problems travel together
studies.ns_score_reason: a clean genetic dissociation between "using" and "becoming dependent", built on very large samples; limited by the abstraction of polygenic methods.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: An Oslo-led team used GWAS summary statistics to separate the genetics of substance *use* (drinks per week, ever using cannabis, smoking initiation, prescription opioid use) from the genetics of substance use *disorders* (alcohol, cannabis, opioid, tobacco), then tested how each related to bipolar disorder. Polygenic scores derived from these latent factors were validated in the Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort Study. Bipolar disorder overlapped strongly with the dependence factor and with a shared use/dependence factor, while the "pure use" factor correlated *negatively* with psychiatric disorders and predicted only self-reported lifetime use. Pathway analysis pointed to dopamine signaling and interneuron function in the shared bipolar–dependence architecture.
studies.why_it_matters: It undercuts the intuitive story that people with bipolar disorder drink and smoke more because of the illness, and suggests instead an inherited liability specific to dependence — a distinction that matters for how comorbidity is conceptualized and studied.
studies.pitch_angle: The surprise is that the genetic variants nudging people toward *having a drink* are not the ones that link to bipolar disorder — only the ones tied to losing control of it. Open on the long-standing clinical assumption that mania drives excess drinking, then show how the genetics reverses the arrow. Call Kevin O'Connell or Ole Andreassen at the Centre for Precision Psychiatry, University of Oslo.
studies.wider_angle: A feature for a genomics or general-science outlet on GWAS-by-subtraction as a technique — researchers now routinely "subtract" one trait from another to isolate hidden causal signatures, with implications well beyond psychiatry. Frame it as statistical dissection of behavior.
studies.caveats: Observational and genetic-correlation based (cannot establish causation); polygenic scores explain small proportions of variance; GWAS samples are overwhelmingly of European ancestry, so findings may not generalize; MoBa outcomes partly self-reported.

studies.title: Serotonin abnormality blamed on borderline personality disorder turns out to belong to depression
studies.ns_score_reason: a neat reattribution of a well-known brain finding using rare PET data, though group sizes are modest.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Columbia researchers used [11C]WAY-100635 PET to measure serotonin 1A receptor binding across 13 predefined brain regions in people with mood disorders (major depression or bipolar I/II) plus comorbid borderline personality disorder (n=21), mood disorders alone (n=63), and healthy volunteers (n=27). Binding was elevated in the mood disorder groups relative to controls — but post-hoc analysis showed the elevation tracked the mood disorder, not borderline personality disorder. Impulsivity, aggression, depression severity, and suicidal ideation showed no relationship to binding.
studies.why_it_matters: Borderline personality disorder has long been described as a "serotonin" condition, partly on the strength of findings like this; if the signal actually belongs to comorbid depression, that helps explain why SSRIs, which act on the 5-HT1A autoreceptor, work for mood disorders but disappoint in borderline personality disorder.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the reversal — the serotonin signature attributed to borderline personality disorder for years appears to be depression hiding inside the comorbidity. Open on the clinical reality that most people diagnosed with borderline personality disorder are prescribed antidepressants that barely help. Call M. Elizabeth Sublette or J. John Mann at the New York State Psychiatric Institute.
studies.wider_angle: For a psychiatry-focused or long-read outlet: the comorbidity confound problem across biological psychiatry — how many "biomarkers" for one diagnosis are really markers of the second diagnosis in the same patients? Use this as the worked example.
studies.caveats: Small comorbid subgroup (n=21), cross-sectional, single-center, secondary post-hoc analysis of pooled PET cohorts; several authors report royalties and industry ties (see disclosure) though unrelated to this work.

studies.title: More data beats smarter algorithms when predicting bipolar disorder in children
studies.ns_score_reason: a well-designed head-to-head test that punctures AI hype in psychiatry; the topic is technical but the message is sharp.
studies.the_study: Researchers compared a simple clinical nomogram, standard statistics (logistic regression, LASSO), four machine-learning models, and a deep-learning neural network for predicting pediatric bipolar disorder, using two independent samples: an academic clinic (N=550) and a community clinic (N=511). All models performed well within the dataset they were trained on and dropped substantially when applied to the other setting. Adding complexity did not help; training on pooled, heterogeneous data did. A single parent-report screening measure, PGBI-10M, was consistently the strongest predictor across every model.
studies.why_it_matters: It is direct evidence that the bottleneck in psychiatric prediction is the diversity of data, not the sophistication of the model — a corrective to the assumption that deep learning will crack diagnosis.
studies.pitch_angle: Sell the deflation: a neural network was no better at spotting bipolar disorder in children than a questionnaire a parent fills in, and every model got worse the moment it left the clinic it was trained in. Open on the mismatch between academic and community clinics, where the same child could be scored differently. Call Eric Youngstrom at Nationwide Children's Hospital.
studies.wider_angle: For a technology or health-policy outlet: "dataset shift" as the quiet failure mode of clinical AI, with the case for open, pooled psychiatric datasets — and the governance and privacy fights that would entail.
studies.caveats: Two US clinical samples only, so population may not generalize; retrospective secondary analysis of existing cohorts; posted earlier as a medRxiv preprint; several authors declare extensive industry and commercial interests (see disclosure), including consultancy on psychological assessment.

studies.title: Most people with bipolar depression would not qualify for the trials that produced their treatment guidelines
studies.ns_score_reason: a striking, readable number with a strong dose-response, undercut by modest sample size and self-rated outcomes.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Clinicians in Naples applied a Trial Eligibility Index to 122 outpatients being treated for acute bipolar depression, asking how many would have been enrolled in the average randomized controlled trial behind current guidelines. Only 43.4% would have been eligible. Those who would have qualified had nearly ten times the odds of reporting that their medication had helped (OR=9.83, 95% CI 4.17–23.18), a result that held across different eligibility thresholds.
studies.why_it_matters: It quantifies something clinicians suspect but rarely measure — the patients seen in real clinics are messier than trial participants, and the guideline evidence may simply not describe them.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is the arithmetic: fewer than half of real bipolar depression patients resemble the people the drug evidence was built on, and the other half report far less benefit. Open on a composite patient with the comorbidities — substance use, medical illness, suicidality — that get you excluded from trials. Call Michele Fornaro at University of Naples Federico II.
studies.wider_angle: For a health-policy or medical outlet: the generalizability crisis across medicine, from oncology to cardiology, and the growing push for pragmatic trials with deliberately broad eligibility. This study is a psychiatric datapoint in a much bigger argument.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional and observational (cannot establish causation); N=122, single center; primary outcome is patient-perceived improvement, i.e. self-reported and unblinded; senior author reports extensive pharmaceutical advisory and honorarium relationships (Janssen, Lundbeck, Otsuka and others).

studies.title: Stimulating the balance organ changes how quickly you recognize your own face
studies.ns_score_reason: genuinely novel causal link between the inner ear and self-recognition, but N=50 and effects are reaction-time-level.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Fifty healthy volunteers did explicit and implicit face-recognition tasks while receiving sinusoidal galvanic vestibular stimulation — weak current across the mastoids that fools the balance system — or sham. Everyone showed the usual "self advantage", recognizing their own face fastest. But stimulation polarity mattered: right-anodal current slowed self-face recognition, while left-anodal current slowed recognition of strangers and sped up recognition of familiar others, erasing the self advantage and converting it into a general familiarity effect.
studies.why_it_matters: It provides causal evidence that the vestibular system — usually filed under balance and spatial orientation — contributes to the sense of self at the level of face identity, extending vestibular contributions to bodily self-representation into the domain of who you recognize as "me".
studies.pitch_angle: The surprise is bodily: nudge the balance organ with a mild current and the privileged status of your own face in your brain quietly dissolves into ordinary familiarity. Open with the volunteer sitting in front of a screen, electrodes behind the ears, unable to say why their own face suddenly feels no more special than a friend's. Call Roberto Gammeri or Raffaella Ricci at the SAN Lab, University of Turin.
studies.wider_angle: For a features desk or a neurology-focused outlet: what vestibular disorders do to the sense of self — patients with chronic dizziness frequently report depersonalization, and this line of work offers a mechanism. A patient-led piece on the underexplored psychiatry of the inner ear.
studies.caveats: Small N (50) split across two polarity groups; healthy volunteers only; reaction-time effects appeared in the explicit task only; short-lived laboratory manipulation with no follow-up.

studies.title: Two stages of treatment-resistant depression turn out to be two different conditions
studies.ns_score_reason: large prospective inpatient cohort with a clear split, but the finding is a refinement of an existing staging idea rather than a new one.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers in Milan prospectively followed 538 depressed inpatients, classifying them as non-resistant, TRD1 (two or more failed antidepressants at minimum licensed dose) or TRD2 (two or more failures across different drug classes at maximum tolerated dose), and tracked symptoms at admission and at 2, 4 and 8 weeks. TRD1 patients (24%) had earlier illness onset and far more personality disorders, anxiety, smoking and substance use — yet improved at a normal rate. Only TRD2 patients (29%) showed genuinely blunted improvement over eight weeks.
studies.why_it_matters: "Treatment-resistant" is currently a single label attached to roughly a third of depressed patients; this suggests it lumps together a complicated-but-responsive group with a biologically stubborn one, which matters for who gets offered ketamine, ECT or neuromodulation.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the split: half of what psychiatry calls treatment resistance may be complexity, not resistance — patients whose depression sits alongside anxiety, addiction and personality difficulties, and who improve fine once treated properly. Open on the label itself and what it does to a patient's expectations. Call Raffaella Zanardi at IRCCS San Raffaele Turro, Milan.
studies.wider_angle: For a specialist medical or drug-development outlet: how the definition of treatment-resistant depression is being rewritten just as billion-dollar drugs (esketamine, psilocybin, neuromodulation devices) are being licensed against it — and what a shifting denominator does to efficacy claims.
studies.caveats: Observational, single-center inpatient cohort (cannot establish causation); naturalistic treatment, so groups received different interventions by design; eight-week follow-up only; results may not generalize to outpatients.

studies.title: Veterans with PTSD improve faster in borderline personality disorder therapy, not slower
studies.ns_score_reason: a useful contradiction of the "too complex to treat" assumption, but small and uncontrolled.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Sixty-two US veterans entering full-model dialectical behavior therapy at a VA medical center were tracked; 31 had probable or confirmed PTSD alongside borderline personality disorder symptoms. Comorbid PTSD did not predict worse baseline severity, worse engagement, or worse outcomes. In fact, veterans with both conditions showed steeper reductions in borderline symptoms over the course of treatment than those without PTSD.
studies.why_it_matters: Much of the evidence for DBT comes from trials with deliberately clean diagnostic profiles — often excluding bipolar disorder and other comorbidities — and clinicians frequently assume complex patients will do worse. Here, the complex patients did at least as well.
studies.pitch_angle: The counterintuitive line is that the "hardest" patients were not the hardest: veterans carrying both trauma and borderline symptoms dropped their symptoms faster in a therapy designed for only one of them. Open on the routine gatekeeping that excludes complex patients from trials — and sometimes from treatment. Call Allison Schreiber at the University of Kentucky College of Medicine.
studies.wider_angle: For a health or veterans-affairs outlet: the diagnostic-purity problem in psychotherapy research, and what happens when treatments developed on tidy samples meet the people who actually turn up at the clinic. Could run with data on trial exclusion rates across psychotherapy RCTs.
studies.caveats: Small N (62); no control or comparison arm — everyone received DBT, so improvement cannot be attributed to therapy with confidence; single VA center; outcomes self-reported; PTSD diagnosis was "probable" in most cases; regression to the mean is a plausible partial explanation for steeper decline in the more symptomatic group.

studies.title: Bipolar disorder and schizophrenia look identical in blood tests at the first psychotic episode
studies.journal: International Journal of Psychiatry in Clinical Practice
studies.ns_score_reason: the null result between diagnoses is the interesting part, but the design is cross-sectional and the markers are crude.
studies.the_study: Turkish researchers analyzed routine blood counts taken within 48 hours of admission from 68 medication-naive patients hospitalized for a first psychotic episode during mania in bipolar disorder, 55 with schizophrenia spectrum disorders, and 61 matched healthy controls. Both patient groups showed raised white cells, neutrophils, monocytes and monocyte-to-lymphocyte ratios versus controls — but were indistinguishable from each other. Only two small differences separated them from controls in a condition-specific way: lower red cell counts in bipolar disorder, lower eosinophils in schizophrenia.
studies.why_it_matters: It adds to evidence that low-grade immune activation accompanies psychosis regardless of which diagnosis is eventually given, which cuts against hopes that simple inflammatory markers could triage bipolar disorder from schizophrenia at first presentation.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is the failure: routine blood work picks up inflammation in first-episode psychosis but cannot tell bipolar disorder from schizophrenia — the diagnostic distinction clinicians agonize over for months. Open on the emergency admission where the diagnosis is a coin flip. Call Esra Uzun Uysal at Bakırköy Training and Research Hospital, Istanbul.
studies.wider_angle: For a science or medical outlet: the immuno-psychiatry story at mid-life — a decade after inflammation became the hot hypothesis in mood disorders, what has it actually delivered? A stock-take feature, and a natural pairing with the ongoing childhood-inflammation cohort work.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional and observational; single-center; retrospective use of routine hemogram records; acute hospitalization, stress and physical illness all affect white cell counts and are hard to exclude; small differences of uncertain clinical meaning; population may not generalize.

studies.title: Shame about a bipolar diagnosis damages daily functioning through a specific route
studies.ns_score_reason: a clear mediation result on an underserved population, but cross-sectional and largely confirmatory of stigma research.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers assessed 110 Tunisian adults with bipolar disorder in remission on internalized stigma, coping style, functioning, self-esteem, cognitive insight and perceived social support. A quarter had clinically significant internalized stigma, with alienation and social withdrawal the strongest components. Mediation analysis showed the link between internalized stigma and poorer functioning ran specifically through perceived devaluation and discrimination — not through coping style, insight, self-esteem or social support, none of which mediated anything.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests that the functional cost of stigma in bipolar disorder is carried by the expectation of being devalued by others, rather than by how people cope or how much support they have — a pointer to which target interventions should aim at, though only a pointer.
studies.pitch_angle: The finding worth leading on is what *didn't* matter: self-esteem, social support and coping strategies all failed to buffer the effect of internalized stigma on functioning, while the belief that other people look down on you did the damage. Open on a person in full remission who still won't tell an employer. Call Bochra Nourhène Saguem at the University of Sousse.
studies.wider_angle: For a global-health or social-science outlet: mental illness stigma outside the Anglophone research bubble. Almost all stigma instruments were developed in North America and Europe; this study asks what they measure in a Tunisian clinic, and whether anti-stigma campaigns designed elsewhere would transfer.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional (mediation here is statistical, not causal); N=110, single site; all measures self-reported; remitted outpatients in one Tunisian region may not generalize.

studies.title: Loading the dose of a long-acting antipsychotic upfront shortens hospital stays for women
studies.ns_score_reason: clinically relevant and sex-specific, but retrospective, small and non-randomized.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: A retrospective cohort of 87 female inpatients with schizophrenia or bipolar disorder in Istanbul compared two ways of starting long-acting injectable aripiprazole: the standard single injection plus 14 days of oral tablets, versus a newer two-injection start with a single 20 mg oral dose. The two-injection group left hospital sooner (8.1 vs 11.8 days), were less likely to be readmitted within a year (17.0% vs 37.5%), and took longer to relapse when they did.
studies.why_it_matters: Long-acting injections exist precisely because taking daily tablets is hard; a regimen that removes the two-week oral overlap could remove a real point of failure — but this is early, non-randomized evidence in women only.
studies.pitch_angle: The angle is the two-week gap nobody talks about: patients are discharged on an injection *plus* a fortnight of pills, and that fortnight is where adherence breaks. Frame around the discharge day and the tablet box that goes unopened. Call Ahmet Ucok at Moodist Psychiatry Hospital, Istanbul. Do not present this as grounds for changing prescribing.
studies.wider_angle: For a pharmacy or medicines-focused outlet: the near-total absence of sex-stratified data in antipsychotic dosing, despite well-documented differences in metabolism, body composition and prolactin effects. This study is unusual simply for being all-female.
studies.caveats: Retrospective, non-randomized cohort (cannot establish causation); small N (87); single-center; female inpatients only, so results may not generalize to men or outpatients; clinicians chose the regimen, so allocation was likely confounded by patient characteristics; adverse events poorly documented.

studies.title: Memory circuits go wrong in different ways in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder
studies.ns_score_reason: a careful direct comparison of two disorders rarely scanned side by side, but the effects are subtle and the story is technical.
studies.the_study: Montreal researchers compared functional connectivity of six hippocampal subregions — anterior, mid and posterior on each side — in people with schizophrenia, people with bipolar disorder, and healthy controls, both at rest and during memory tasks. Some abnormalities were shared: reduced connectivity between the right mid-hippocampus and temporal cortex appeared in both disorders. Others were specific: hyperconnectivity between the right posterior hippocampus and inferior temporal gyrus occurred only in schizophrenia. One anterior hippocampal pattern was schizophrenia-specific at rest but shared once participants were actually doing a memory task.
studies.why_it_matters: Treating the hippocampus as a single structure has blurred the differences between these two diagnoses; splitting it along its long axis, and scanning during a task rather than at rest, reveals overlap and divergence that resting-state work alone misses.
studies.pitch_angle: The nice detail is context-dependence — one brain difference looked specific to schizophrenia when participants lay still, and stopped being specific the moment they were asked to remember something. Use that to open on the limits of resting-state brain imaging. Call Stéphane Potvin at the Institut Universitaire en Santé Mentale de Montréal.
studies.wider_angle: For a neuroscience-literate outlet: the long-axis hippocampus as an idea — the growing evidence that its front and back ends do quite different jobs (emotion and context versus fine spatial and episodic detail), and what that reorganization is doing to memory research generally.
studies.caveats: Sample sizes not stated in the abstract and likely modest for imaging; cross-sectional and observational; participants almost certainly medicated, a persistent confound in psychiatric neuroimaging; multiple seeds and two contexts raise multiple-comparison concerns; single-center.

feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Five studies in this batch converge on the same problem from different directions — psychiatric evidence is built on unusually tidy patients, and it does not survive contact with the messy ones. "Most people with bipolar depression would not qualify for the trials that produced their treatment guidelines" (PMID 42575197) puts a number on the exclusion (43.4% eligible, with the eligible group nearly ten times more likely to say their medication helped); "Serotonin abnormality blamed on borderline personality disorder turns out to belong to depression" (PMID 42173043) shows a signature biomarker was really a second diagnosis hiding in the comorbidity; "Veterans with PTSD improve faster in borderline personality disorder therapy, not slower" (PMID 41084836) and "Two stages of treatment-resistant depression turn out to be two different conditions" (PMID 41904070) both find that the "complicated" patients routinely screened out of research do fine, or fine for reasons the label obscures; and "More data beats smarter algorithms when predicting bipolar disorder in children" (PMID 42600789) shows prediction models trained in an academic clinic degrade the moment they meet a community one.

**Why pitch this now:** Guidelines, diagnostic labels and a new generation of prediction tools are all being written and licensed on samples that describe a minority of the people who actually turn up in clinics — and this batch is the first time the size of that gap has been quantified across drugs, therapy, biomarkers and algorithms at once.

**Angle:** A reported feature following one composite, entirely ordinary patient — bipolar depression plus a drinking problem, some trauma history, a personality disorder diagnosis — through every stage where the evidence base quietly stops applying to them: the trial they can't enroll in, the biomarker that belongs to someone else's diagnosis, the algorithm trained down the road, the label that predicts their prognosis wrongly. For a general science-literate audience interested in how medical evidence gets made, not just what it says.

**Potential headlines:**
- Fewer than half of bipolar depression patients match the trials behind their prescriptions
- The patients psychiatry calls too complicated to study keep doing better than expected
- Your diagnosis has a research double, and the evidence was written for them

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Features** — has the room for a multi-study, mechanism-plus-policy piece and an audience already primed by coverage of replication and generalizability problems in medicine.
- **STAT** — the trial-eligibility arithmetic and the "shifting denominator" for treatment-resistant depression land directly in their drug-development and regulatory beat, especially with esketamine and psilocybin being licensed against that very label.
- **Undark** — well suited to the critical, methods-forward framing of how exclusion criteria and comorbidity confounds shape what psychiatry believes it knows.
- **Wired** — would take the dataset-shift strand (PMID 42600789) as the spine, with the trial-eligibility work as evidence that clinical AI inherits an older problem rather than solving it.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: New Scientist Story Ideas — Bipolar — September 2026
**Checked:** 2026-09-07 | **Studies reviewed:** 11
**Publication:** New Scientist | **Section:** New Scientist Mind

---

### Study 1: Genes for addiction — not for drinking or smoking as such — explain why bipolar disorder and substance problems travel together
**PMID:** 42636965 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Why it matters" makes a claim the design cannot test** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "It undercuts the intuitive story that people with bipolar disorder drink and smoke more because of the illness, and suggests instead an inherited liability specific to dependence"
- **Abstract says:** "By dissecting the genetic liability to SUD and SU and investigating their relationship with BIP we find a genetic signature correlated with substance dependence but not substance use more broadly."
- **Problem:** The study partitions shared genetic architecture; it does not test whether the illness itself drives increased consumption. Finding that shared genetics loads onto dependence rather than use does not "undercut" a behavioral, illness-driven pathway to heavier drinking or smoking — the two explanations can coexist.
- **Suggested fix:** "It suggests that what bipolar disorder shares genetically with substance problems is a liability to dependence rather than to consumption itself — a distinction that matters for how comorbidity is conceptualized and studied."

**Issue B. Causal language in the pitch angle contradicts the digest's own caveat** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "then show how the genetics reverses the arrow"
- **Abstract says:** Polygenic overlap, genetic correlations, GWAS-by-subtraction and PRS associations — no directional or causal analysis (e.g. no Mendelian randomization) is reported.
- **Problem:** "Reverses the arrow" asserts a direction of causation. The caveats correctly state the work "cannot establish causation," so the pitch line contradicts the caveat.
- **Suggested fix:** "then show how the genetics complicates that story: the shared liability sits with dependence, not with consumption."

**Issue C. Overstated dissociation** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the genetic variants nudging people toward *having a drink* are not the ones that link to bipolar disorder"
- **Abstract says:** "We found extensive polygenic overlap between traits, with SUDs being more genetically correlated with BIP than SU traits… The unique SUD factor correlated positively with psychiatric disorders, whereas unique SU correlated negatively."
- **Problem:** Substance-use traits were still genetically correlated with bipolar disorder, just less so, and the residual "unique use" factor correlated *negatively* with psychiatric disorders — which is a link, not an absence of one. "Not the ones that link" reads as zero overlap.
- **Suggested fix:** "the genetic variants nudging people toward *having a drink* are only weakly related to bipolar disorder — and once dependence liability is subtracted out, they point mildly in the opposite direction."

*Note:* The first name "Kevin" for O'Connell KS is unverifiable from the abstract alone (the abstract gives initials only).

---

### Study 2: Serotonin abnormality blamed on borderline personality disorder turns out to belong to depression
**PMID:** 42173043 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. NS fit score sits on a very small, post-hoc subgroup** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**NS fit:** 7/10 — a neat reattribution of a well-known brain finding using rare PET data, though group sizes are modest."
- **Abstract says:** "comorbid BPD (n = 21)… the groups differed significantly in binding potential (BPF)… (F = 3.64; p = 0.03). Planned post-hoc analyses found that these differences… were driven by higher binding associated with mood disorder, and not with BPD."
- **Problem:** The central claim rests on a 21-person comorbid subgroup and a planned post-hoc contrast off a borderline primary result (p = 0.03 across 13 a priori regions). That is thin support for a 7, even with objective PET measurement.
- **Suggested fix:** "**NS fit:** 6/10 — a neat reattribution of a well-known brain finding using rare PET data, but the key contrast is post-hoc and the comorbid group is only 21 people."

**Issue B. Prescribing claim not in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Open on the clinical reality that most people diagnosed with borderline personality disorder are prescribed antidepressants that barely help."
- **Abstract says:** Only that SSRIs "are effective for mood disorders but have limited efficacy for BPD."
- **Problem:** The "most people… are prescribed" prevalence claim is Unverifiable from abstract only, and would need separate sourcing before it appears in a pitch.
- **Suggested fix:** "Open on the clinical puzzle that SSRIs, widely used in borderline personality disorder, show limited efficacy for it [sourcing needed for prescribing rates]."

---

### Study 3: More data beats smarter algorithms when predicting bipolar disorder in children
**PMID:** 42600789 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Direct evidence" overstates a hedged, within-study conclusion** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "It is direct evidence that the bottleneck in psychiatric prediction is the diversity of data, not the sophistication of the model"
- **Abstract says:** "Within the present study, increasing model complexity did not improve external performance, whereas training on pooled data improved performance on held-out samples from the heterogeneous pooled cohort. These findings suggest that training-data diversity may provide greater practical benefit…"
- **Problem:** The authors twice hedge ("within the present study", "may provide"). Crucially, pooled training improved performance on held-out samples *from the pooled cohort* — not demonstrated cross-setting transfer — so "the bottleneck is diversity of data" is an inference, not a direct demonstration.
- **Suggested fix:** "Within these two datasets, added model complexity bought nothing externally, while training on pooled data helped on held-out samples from the combined cohort — which the authors read as evidence that data diversity may matter more than model sophistication."

**Issue B. Pitch hook rests on a comparison the abstract doesn't report** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "a neural network was no better at spotting bipolar disorder in children than a questionnaire a parent fills in"
- **Abstract says:** "all models showed good internal discrimination in the academic dataset… Across models and training strategies, PGBI-10M was consistently identified as the most important predictor."
- **Problem:** Being the top-ranked predictor inside multivariable models is not the same as a head-to-head test of PGBI-10M alone against the multilayer perceptron. The abstract reports no such single-item-versus-deep-learning comparison.
- **Suggested fix:** "a deep-learning model did no better than a simple clinical nomogram or plain logistic regression, and in every model the single strongest predictor was a parent-completed questionnaire."

**Issue C. Direction of the generalization failure** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "All models performed well within the dataset they were trained on and dropped substantially when applied to the other setting… every model got worse the moment it left the clinic it was trained in"
- **Abstract says:** "all models showed good internal discrimination in the academic dataset, but external discrimination in the community dataset substantially declined."
- **Problem:** The abstract specifies one direction (academic → community). Whether the reverse transfer also degraded is Unverifiable from abstract only, so the bidirectional phrasing is unsupported.
- **Suggested fix:** "All models performed well in the academic dataset they were trained on, and discrimination dropped substantially when they were applied to the community clinic."

---

### Study 4: Most people with bipolar depression would not qualify for the trials that produced their treatment guidelines
**PMID:** 42575197 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Composite-patient detail not sourced from the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Open on a composite patient with the comorbidities — substance use, medical illness, suicidality — that get you excluded from trials."
- **Abstract says:** "The continuous TEI was associated with several psychiatric and medical characteristics in multivariable analysis."
- **Problem:** The specific exclusion drivers named (substance use, medical illness, suicidality) are not itemized in the abstract. Unverifiable from abstract only — plausible, but needs full text before it goes in a pitch.
- **Suggested fix:** "Open on a composite patient carrying the psychiatric and medical comorbidities that lowered TEI scores in this cohort [confirm specifics against full text]."

**Issue B. "Held across different eligibility thresholds" flattens a weak sensitivity result** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "a result that held across different eligibility thresholds"
- **Abstract says:** "Sensitivity analyses produced the same classification at a cutoff of 70 and preserved the direction of association at a cutoff of 80 (OR = 9.33, 95%CI 1.14–76.09; p = 0.013)."
- **Problem:** At the 80 cutoff the confidence interval runs from 1.14 to 76.09 — the direction survives but the estimate is extremely imprecise. "Held" implies robustness the numbers don't quite support.
- **Suggested fix:** "the direction of the effect survived at stricter and looser thresholds, though with much wider uncertainty at the strictest cutoff (OR = 9.33, 95% CI 1.14–76.09)."

---

### Study 5: Stimulating the balance organ changes how quickly you recognize your own face
**PMID:** 42276516 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Scene-setting implies a subjective change that wasn't measured** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "unable to say why their own face suddenly feels no more special than a friend's"
- **Abstract says:** "under L-GVS RTs for self-faces no longer differ from those of familiar-other faces, effectively shifting the SA toward a more general familiarity advantage."
- **Problem:** The finding is a reaction-time equivalence in an explicit recognition task. No subjective or phenomenological report is described, so the "feels no more special" framing invents an experience the study didn't assess.
- **Suggested fix:** "unable to notice that their own face has stopped being the fastest one they recognize."

**Issue B. Study has no connection to the digest's stated focus** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**Focus:** bipolar" (digest header) / "sinusoidal galvanic vestibular stimulation"
- **Abstract says:** "while receiving sinusoidal bipolar GVS or Sham stimulation."
- **Problem:** This paper appears to have entered a bipolar-focused screen via the electrode configuration term "bipolar GVS," not because it concerns bipolar disorder. Not a factual error in the write-up, but worth flagging so the section editor knows the entry is off-topic for the stated brief.
- **Suggested fix:** Retain only if the desk wants a standalone Mind item; otherwise drop from a bipolar-focused digest.

### Study 6: Two stages of treatment-resistant depression turn out to be two different conditions
**PMID:** 41904070 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline overstates "two different conditions"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Two stages of treatment-resistant depression turn out to be two different conditions"
- **Abstract says:** "a simple two-stage TRD model differentiated a 'complex but responsive' subgroup (TRD1) from a more biologically refractory profile (TRD2)."
- **Problem:** The authors describe two clinical *profiles* within depression, distinguished by comorbidity burden and improvement trajectory. "Two different conditions" implies distinct nosological entities, which the data do not establish.
- **Suggested fix:** "Two stages of treatment-resistant depression look like two very different clinical profiles"

**Issue B. Prevalence figure doesn't match this cohort** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "'Treatment-resistant' is currently a single label attached to roughly a third of depressed patients"
- **Abstract says:** "TRD1 patients (24%)… TRD2 patients (29%)" — i.e. 53% of this inpatient cohort met one of the two TRD definitions.
- **Problem:** The "roughly a third" figure is a general literature estimate that sits awkwardly next to a study in which over half the sample was classified as treatment-resistant. Readers will assume the number comes from this paper.
- **Suggested fix:** "'Treatment-resistant' is currently a single label — one that covered more than half of this inpatient cohort (24% TRD1, 29% TRD2)."

*Note:* The digest's TRD definitions omit the "for ≥4 weeks" duration requirement in both tiers; not an error, but worth restoring if space allows.

### Study 8: Bipolar disorder and schizophrenia look identical in blood tests at the first psychotic episode
**PMID:** 42112712 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline runs against the authors' own conclusion** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Bipolar disorder and schizophrenia look identical in blood tests at the first psychotic episode"
- **Abstract says:** "No significant differences in blood cell counts or inflammatory markers were found between bipolar disorder and schizophrenia spectrum groups… Condition-specific findings, like decreased RBCs in bipolar disorder and eosinophils in schizophrenia, suggest unique early haematological profiles."
- **Problem:** The direct between-group comparison was null — so the headline is defensible — but the authors emphasize condition-specific profiles versus controls and conclude the opposite of "identical." The body text handles this fairly; the headline does not, and an editor should know the paper's own spin points the other way.
- **Suggested fix:** "Bipolar disorder and schizophrenia can't be told apart on routine blood tests at the first psychotic episode"

### Study 9: Shame about a bipolar diagnosis damages daily functioning through a specific route
**PMID:** 42113129 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Self-esteem and social support were tested on a different relationship** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "not through coping style, insight, self-esteem or social support, none of which mediated anything" / "self-esteem, social support and coping strategies all failed to buffer the effect of internalized stigma on functioning"
- **Abstract says:** "Stigma coping strategies and cognitive insight did not significantly mediate this relationship. Cognitive insight, self-esteem, or perceived social support did not exhibit a significant effect on the relationship between internalized stigma and coping strategies."
- **Problem:** Only coping strategies and cognitive insight were reported as non-mediators of the stigma→functioning path. Self-esteem and perceived social support were reported as having no effect on the stigma→*coping* relationship — a different model. The digest merges the two, and the pitch hook ("what *didn't* matter") depends on that merge.
- **Suggested fix:** "Mediation analysis showed the link between internalized stigma and poorer functioning ran specifically through perceived devaluation and discrimination — not through coping style or cognitive insight. Self-esteem, cognitive insight and social support were separately tested and did not shape the stigma–coping relationship either." Rework the pitch hook accordingly.

**Issue B. Causal headline for cross-sectional mediation** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Shame about a bipolar diagnosis damages daily functioning through a specific route"
- **Abstract says:** "A cross-sectional study was conducted… Internalized stigma experienced by individuals with bipolar disorder negatively impacts functioning through a heightened perception of discrimination and devaluation."
- **Problem:** "Damages" asserts causation from cross-sectional mediation, contradicting the digest's own caveat that "mediation here is statistical, not causal." (The authors use similar language, but that doesn't license it in a headline.) Separately, "shame" is a loose gloss on internalized stigma, whose most elevated domains here were alienation and social withdrawal.
- **Suggested fix:** "Internalized stigma tracks poorer functioning in bipolar disorder — via one specific route"

### Study 10: Loading the dose of a long-acting antipsychotic upfront shortens hospital stays for women
**PMID:** 41924987 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Causal headline for a retrospective, non-randomized cohort** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Loading the dose of a long-acting antipsychotic upfront shortens hospital stays for women"
- **Abstract says:** "This retrospective cohort study included 87 female inpatients… Aripiprazole monohydrate LAI initiation with the TIS regimen was associated with shorter hospitalization and more favorable rehospitalization outcomes."
- **Problem:** "Shortens" states cause. The authors say "was associated with," and the digest's own caveats note that clinicians chose the regimen, so allocation was likely confounded. The headline contradicts the caveat.
- **Suggested fix:** "A two-injection start for a long-acting antipsychotic is linked to shorter hospital stays in women"

**Issue B. Outcome variable renamed** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "and took longer to relapse when they did"
- **Abstract says:** "time to rehospitalization was longer (P = 0.027)."
- **Problem:** The measured outcome is time to rehospitalization, not relapse. Relapse without readmission would not be captured, so the substitution broadens the claim.
- **Suggested fix:** "and took longer to be readmitted when they were"

### Study 11: Memory circuits go wrong in different ways in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder
**PMID:** 42679550 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. The six long-axis seeds, the two contexts, the shared right mid-hippocampal hypoconnectivity, the schizophrenia-specific right posterior–inferior temporal gyrus hyperconnectivity, and the context-dependent right anterior pattern all match the abstract. The caveat that sample sizes are not reported in the abstract is appropriately honest, and the "participants almost certainly medicated" line is correctly presented as an assumption rather than a finding.
